title: The Gods of Seir
sum: Amaziah does what is right, "but not with a whole heart." He executes his father's murderers but spares their children, as the Law of Moses commands. Preparing for war with Edom, he hires a hundred thousand soldiers from Israel; a man of God warns that the LORD is not with Ephraim, and Amaziah sends them home at the cost of his silver. The angry mercenaries raid Judah's towns. Amaziah wins in the Valley of Salt, then brings back Edom's gods and worships them.

A prophet asks why he would seek gods that could not save their own people, and Amaziah silences him. Proud of his victory, he challenges Joash of Israel, who answers with a fable of a thornbush and a cedar. Judah is routed at Beth-shemesh, Jerusalem's wall is breached and the temple treasure taken. From the time he turned away, a plot follows him to Lachish, where he is killed.
readings: Read as history

The outline matches 2 Kings 14: Amaziah's revenge on his father's killers, the victory over Edom, the defeat by Joash and the conspiracy. Chronicles adds the hired northern army and the Edomite gods. Some historians think the mercenaries reflect a real treaty; others see a story told to make a point about trusting God rather than numbers.
Read as a sermon

Chronicles turns the reign into a lesson in two halves. Amaziah obeys the prophet, loses his silver and wins; then he takes up defeated gods, rejects a prophet and loses everything. The prophet's words "God's counsel is to destroy you" (25:16) answer the king's "Is it the king's counselor we have made you?" The narrator dates the plot "from the time Amaziah turned away" (25:27).

views.H: Amaziah's reign rises and falls on his heart. The man of God tells him, "With God is the strength to help or to make stumble" (25:8), and the king's choices prove it: obedience at cost brings victory, idolatry and pride bring defeat.
views.C: Chronicles has reshaped 2 Kings 14:1–20 around its theology of reward and punishment. The added episodes, the hired army and the gods of Seir, explain why a king Kings calls good suffered disaster. The figures (300,000 men, 10,000 thrown from the rock) are typical of the Chronicler's large numbers.
views.S: Kings says Amaziah "did what was right in the LORD's eyes, only not like David" (2 Kings 14:3); Chronicles says "not with a whole heart." Kings has no Edomite gods and no prophets; Joash's fable and the battle are copied almost word for word. Kings places the plot fifteen years later without explanation; Chronicles links it to his turning away.
views.J: Rabbinic readers noted Amaziah's obedience to Deuteronomy 24:16 as praise: he followed the written Law even in revenge. Jewish interpreters asked why a victor would worship the gods of the defeated; the usual answer is the prophet's own: idolatry makes no sense, and that is the point of the story (25:15).
views.X: Christian preachers have used the hired army as a lesson in trusting God over resources: "It is in the LORD's power to give you far beyond this" (25:9). Joash's thistle fable has been compared to Jesus' warnings against pride before a fall.

deep.h: Why worship the gods you defeated?
deep.b: Amaziah brings back the gods of Seir after beating Edom (25:14). Ancient conquerors did take the gods of the conquered, but usually as trophies, to show their own gods' power, as the Philistines carried off the ark (1 Samuel 5:1–2). Worshiping such gods made little sense, as the prophet says (25:15). Some historians suggest he wanted to win over the gods of a newly conquered territory. Chronicles' point is the irony: gods that could not save their own people are no help to anyone.

deep.title: A story about the north
deep.b: Claude's theory. Chronicles is often thought hostile to the northern kingdom, yet in this chapter the man of God says only that the LORD is not with Israel's army, not that northerners are lost. The returned mercenaries' violence (25:13) sets up the very different behavior of northern leaders in 28:9–15. Perhaps the Chronicler wanted his readers to see that the same people could do great harm or great good. This is close to H. G. M. Williamson's argument in Israel in the Books of Chronicles (1977) that Chronicles keeps the north within Israel; the pairing of 25:13 with 28:9–15 is my own emphasis.

settings.by: Moses, quoted from 'the book of Moses' (Deuteronomy 24:16)
settings.to: Israel's judges and kings; here applied by Amaziah
settings.when: When Amaziah executed his father's murderers but spared their sons
settings.why: The same scene and the same quotation as 2 Kings 14:6. In Kings it praises Amaziah for keeping Moses' law. Chronicles keeps it as the first sign of a king who did right 'only not with an undivided heart' (25:2). It also fits the Chronicler's whole view that each generation answers for its own sin. For readers who did not want to carry their ancestors' guilt, the law was good news.

settings.what: The man of God and the hired troops
settings.by: An unnamed man of God; Amaziah
settings.to: Amaziah; the man of God
settings.when: Before Amaziah's war with Edom
settings.why: 'The LORD is not with Israel.' The prophet tells Amaziah to send home the 100,000 men hired from the north. When the king worries about the silver, he answers, 'It is in the LORD's power to give you far beyond this.' Readers learn to trust God over money and to keep apart from the north's kingdom, if not from its people.

settings.what: The prophet's rebuke of Amaziah's idols
settings.by: A prophet; then Amaziah
settings.to: Amaziah; then the prophet
settings.when: After Amaziah brought home and worshiped the gods of Seir
settings.why: 'Why go seeking the gods of this people? They could not rescue their own people.' The king silences him, and the prophet says God's counsel is to destroy him. The exchange explains the defeat that follows. For readers it mocked the folly of serving gods already beaten.

settings.by: Amaziah king of Judah; then Joash king of Israel
settings.to: Each other, by messengers
settings.when: After Amaziah's victory over Edom, about 790 BC
settings.why: The same scene and fable as 2 Kings 14:8–10: the thornbush, the cedar and the trampling beast. In Kings the fable mocks a king's pride. Chronicles adds that Amaziah's refusal to listen 'came from God... because they had sought the gods of Edom' (25:20). The defeat becomes a judgment on idolatry, not just on pride, which is the lesson Chronicles wants its readers to take.

title: Strong Until He Was Strong
sum: Uzziah becomes king at sixteen and reigns fifty-two years. As long as he seeks God in the days of Zechariah, God makes him prosper. He breaks down the walls of Philistine cities, defeats Arabs and Meunites, receives tribute from Ammon, fortifies Jerusalem, digs cisterns, keeps herds and loves the soil. His army is well equipped, and inventive machines on the towers shoot arrows and stones. His fame spreads, "for help came to him in wonderful ways, until he was strong."

Then his heart rises. He enters the temple to burn incense, and Azariah the chief priest and eighty priests confront him. As he rages with the censer in his hand, skin disease breaks out on his forehead. He lives apart until his death, his son Jotham governing for him, and is buried in a field near, not in, the royal tombs.
readings: Read as history

Kings records Azariah's long reign and his disease in seven verses (2 Kings 15:1–7). Chronicles' extra material, the wars, building and farming, may come from records now lost; Uzziah's seals and a later burial plaque show he was remembered. The temple incident is found only here.
Read as a warning

The chapter is built on the words "help" and "strong," which echo the king's two names. Strength given by God becomes the occasion of a fall. The leprous king, cut off from the house he tried to invade, is a picture of pride undone.

views.H: Uzziah is a good king who forgets where his strength comes from. His sin is to claim a priest's holy work, and the punishment fits: he is barred from the temple for the rest of his life.
views.C: The Chronicler has supplied a cause for the disease Kings mentions without explanation. The story reflects Second Temple concerns about the sanctity of the priesthood and the limits of royal power, as seen in Numbers 16–18.
views.S: Kings calls him Azariah and gives no reason for the disease; Chronicles calls him Uzziah and tells why. Kings has him buried "with his ancestors in the City of David"; Chronicles specifies a field belonging to the kings. The opening notice about Elath (26:2) is copied in its odd position from 2 Kings 14:22.
views.J: Josephus says that at the moment Uzziah entered the temple an earthquake split the temple roof, and a ray of sunlight struck the king's face, bringing the disease (Antiquities 9.222–227). The Rabbis linked the earthquake of Amos 1:1 and Zechariah 14:5 with this day.
views.X: Christian readers have drawn the line between king and priest from this chapter, and have seen it fulfilled only in Christ, who is priest-king after the order of Melchizedek (Hebrews 7). Isaiah's vision "in the year King Uzziah died" (Isaiah 6:1) has been read as the true King appearing after the fall of a proud one.

deep.b: In 1931 the scholar E. L. Sukenik published a limestone plaque found in the collection of the Russian monastery on the Mount of Olives. Its Aramaic inscription, in a script of about the first century BC or AD, reads: "Here were brought the bones of Uzziah king of Judah. Do not open." It shows that in Second Temple times Uzziah's grave was known and his remains were moved, perhaps because Jerusalem was expanding. The plaque is in the Israel Museum.

echoes: 2 Kings 14:21–22; 2 Kings 15:1–7; Isaiah 6:1; Amos 1:1; Zechariah 14:5; Numbers 16:40; Numbers 12:10; Exodus 28:36–38

settings.by: Azariah the priest and eighty priests of the LORD
settings.to: King Uzziah, inside the Temple at the incense altar
settings.when: When Uzziah, at the height of his power, went in to burn incense
settings.why: 'It is not your place to burn incense to the LORD. That belongs to the priests.' The priests defend the law of Numbers 16:40 and 18:7 against the king. The skin disease that follows explains what Kings leaves unexplained (2 Kings 15:5). For readers whose Temple had priests but no king, the scene set firm limits on any ruler's claim over holy things.

traditions.q: King Uzziah was struck with skin disease for burning incense, a task for priests (2 Chronicles 26:16–21). What power may rulers have over the church?
views: Pope Gelasius I wrote to the emperor in 494 that the world is ruled by two powers, the authority of bishops and the power of kings, and that in sacred things rulers must submit to priests. Today the Church teaches that it is not to be confused in any way with the political community (Catechism 2245).

Byzantine teaching spoke of a harmony (symphonia) between church and empire: the emperor protects the faith and the priests serve at the altar (Justinian, Novel 6, 535). Orthodox churches have since lived under many kinds of states, but have kept the ideal of church and nation working together.

Article 37 gives the monarch chief government over all people in the realm, clergy included, but says rulers may not preach the word or give the sacraments. The British monarch is still Supreme Governor of the Church of England.

The Westminster Confession says rulers may not take on the ministry of word and sacraments, listing Uzziah among its proof texts, but gave them a duty to keep the church's peace and to call synods (23.3). American Presbyterians rewrote the article in 1788 to deny the state any rule over the church.
Church and state should be separate. The state must not favor or control any church, and the church must not use the state to do its work (Baptist Faith and Message 17).

title: Jotham Kept His Ways Steady
sum: Jotham reigns sixteen years and does what is right, as his father did, except that he does not enter the LORD's temple; but the people still act corruptly. He builds the upper gate of the temple and the wall of the Ophel, towns in the hills and forts in the woods. He defeats the Ammonites, who pay tribute for three years.
Jotham grows strong "because he kept his ways steady before the LORD his God." The chapter ends with his regnal formula, repeated from its start.
readings: Read as history

Kings gives Jotham seven verses and notes that the attacks of Rezin and Pekah began in his days (2 Kings 15:37). Chronicles omits this, records a war with Ammon, and lists building works. Jotham probably served as regent during his father's illness, so his reign overlaps Uzziah's.
Read as a model
Jotham is one of the few kings in Chronicles with no recorded fault. The short chapter shows what steady faithfulness looks like, between a father who fell and a son who will be the worst king yet.

views.H: A brief, faithful reign. Jotham avoids his father's sin, builds and wins, and his strength is credited to his steadiness before God.
views.C: Chronicles builds Jotham's reign to fit its pattern, omitting the harassment from Aram and Israel and supplying a victory. The repeated verse (27:8) may be a scribal duplicate.
views.S: Kings' "only" clause about the high places becomes "only he did not go into the temple." The war with Ammon and the building notices beyond the upper gate are not in Kings.
views.J: The Talmud counts Jotham among the truly righteous (Bavli Sukkah 45b), and commentators explain this by his honor for his father: while he governed for Uzziah, he judged in his father's name.
views.X: Jotham appears in Jesus' genealogy (Matthew 1:9). Christian readers have found in him an example of quiet faithfulness that Scripture records without drama.

title: Clothed from the Plunder
sum: Ahaz walks in the ways of Israel's kings: he makes images for the Baals, burns his sons in the Valley of Ben-hinnom and sacrifices at high places. God gives him into the hands of Aram and of Israel. Pekah kills 120,000 in Judah in a day, and the northern army carries 200,000 captives to Samaria. There a prophet, Oded, meets the army: God used you, he says, but your fury has gone too far. Northern leaders agree, and they clothe, feed, anoint and carry the captives to Jericho.

Ahaz turns to Assyria for help, but Tilgath-pilneser only presses him harder. Edomites and Philistines raid Judah. Ahaz sacrifices to the gods of Damascus, breaks up the temple's vessels, shuts its doors and builds altars in every corner of Jerusalem. He is not buried in the royal tombs.
readings: Read as history

The Syro-Ephraimite war of about 734 BC is known from Kings, Isaiah and Assyrian records, which list "Jehoahaz of Judah" among Tiglath-pileser's tributaries. Chronicles reports defeats and captives, not the siege of Jerusalem; the very large numbers are probably not literal.
Read as contrast

The chapter sets Judah's king against northern Samaria. The king of Judah behaves like a northern king; the northerners, rebuked by a prophet, behave like the people of God. The scene of mercy in 28:15 is the center of the chapter.

views.H: Ahaz is the worst of Judah's kings so far, and everything he trusts fails. His only help is refused; his gods make him stumble. Mercy comes from an unexpected source: Israel's soldiers, moved by a prophet.
views.C: Chronicles has turned Ahaz into the type of the apostate king, expanding Kings' charges and closing the temple to prepare for Hezekiah's reopening. The Oded story may express a hope in the Chronicler's own day for better relations with the north.
views.S: Kings tells of Rezin and Pekah's siege of Jerusalem, of Ahaz's appeal and of Assyria's success against Damascus (2 Kings 16:5–9), and of his Damascus-style altar (16:10–16). Chronicles omits the siege and the altar's design, adds the battles, captives and Oded, and judges Assyria's help as no help.
views.J: The Talmud asks why Ahaz is not listed among the kings with no share in the world to come, and answers that he stood between two righteous kings, his father and his son (Bavli Sanhedrin 104a). It also says he shut the houses of study so that Torah would not be taught (Bavli Sanhedrin 103b).
views.X: Some scholars, notably F. Scott Spencer (1984), have seen 28:15 as the source of the Good Samaritan parable (Luke 10:30–37). Ahaz is also the king to whom Isaiah gave the sign of Immanuel (Isaiah 7:14), which Matthew applies to Jesus.

deep.b: Ancient armies often sold captives as slaves. The northern leaders' decision to free their "relatives" (28:8, 28:11) follows the Law's ban on enslaving fellow Israelites (Leviticus 25:39–46). The care described is concrete: clothes and sandals, food and drink, oil for wounds, donkeys for the weak, and safe conduct to Jericho. The four named leaders (28:12) are otherwise unknown, but their names, several with "the LORD" in them, mark them as faithful northerners.

settings.what: Oded's rebuke of the northern army
settings.by: Oded, a prophet of the LORD in Samaria
settings.to: The army of Israel coming home with 200,000 captives from Judah
settings.when: After Pekah's victory over Ahaz, about 734 BC
settings.why: 'Don't you carry guilt of your own?... Return the captives you have taken from your own relatives.' A northern prophet calls northerners to mercy toward their kin in Judah. For readers, the north here is not the enemy but a brother who can still listen.

settings.by: Azariah, Berechiah, Jehizkiah and Amasa, leaders of Ephraim
settings.to: The returning soldiers, before the assembly
settings.when: Right after Oded's words
settings.why: They refuse to bring the captives in, fearing more guilt, and then clothe, feed and return them to Jericho. The scene, told only in Chronicles, shows northerners acting more faithfully than Judah's king Ahaz. Spencer and others argue it lies behind Jesus' parable of the good Samaritan. For the first readers it was a picture of what Israel's brothers in the north could be.

settings.what: Ahaz's reason for serving Aram's gods
settings.by: King Ahaz
settings.to: Spoken as he sacrificed to the gods of Damascus
settings.when: While Ahaz was hard pressed by his enemies
settings.why: 'The gods of Aram's kings help them... To them I will sacrifice, and they will help me.' The narrator answers at once: 'Instead they made him stumble, him and all Israel.' Ahaz is the opposite of the kings who seek the LORD. Readers living among other peoples' gods heard how foolish it is to borrow the gods of whoever seems strong.

title: The Doors Opened
sum: Hezekiah becomes king at twenty-five, and in his first month he opens the temple doors his father shut. He calls the priests and Levites: our fathers turned their backs on the LORD's house, and fury came on us; now I mean to make a covenant with God. The Levites cleanse the temple in sixteen days, carrying the uncleanness out to the Kidron.

Then Hezekiah and the officials go up with seven bulls, rams, lambs and goats for a sin offering for the kingdom, the sanctuary and Judah, for all Israel. The Levites play David's instruments and the priests the trumpets; as the burnt offering begins, so does the song, until all bow down. The people bring thank offerings in such numbers that the Levites help the few priests. "It had all come about in a moment."
readings: Read as history

Kings says Hezekiah removed the high places and trusted God (2 Kings 18:3–6) but does not describe a temple cleansing. Some historians accept Chronicles' account as based on records; others think it imitates Josiah's reform and Second Temple ritual practice.
Read as liturgy

The chapter follows the order of worship: confession, cleansing, atonement, burnt offering with music, thanksgiving. It reads almost like a service book for a rededication, with Levites, priests and king each in their places.

views.H: Hezekiah's faith is shown first in worship. His first act is to reopen the temple and restore the offerings, and the people's joy shows God's hand in it.
views.C: The chapter is the Chronicler's most detailed picture of ideal worship, drawing on the Priestly laws of Leviticus and on the music David arranged in 1 Chronicles 15–16 and 23–26. Its praise of the Levites over the priests (29:34) may reflect tensions in the writer's day.
views.S: Kings has a single summary verse on Hezekiah's reform (2 Kings 18:4). The opening doors, the Levites' speech, the sacrifices and the music are all Chronicles' own. The regnal formula in 29:1–2 matches Kings, with the mother's name Abijah in place of Abi.
views.J: The Talmud praises Hezekiah for teaching Torah so widely that there was no one from Dan to Beersheba ignorant of the laws of purity (Bavli Sanhedrin 94b). Rabbinic readers took the opening of the doors as the beginning of national repentance.
views.X: Christian readers have taken the chapter as a pattern of revival: the doors opened, the house cleansed, atonement made, and worship restored with joy. The sin offering "for all Israel" (29:24) has been read as pointing to Christ's offering for all (Hebrews 9:11–14).

echoes: 2 Kings 18:1–7; Leviticus 4:1–35; Leviticus 16:15–19; 1 Chronicles 15:16–24; 1 Chronicles 25:1–7; Ezekiel 8:16; Hebrews 9:11–14

settings.what: Hezekiah's speech to the priests and Levites
settings.by: Hezekiah king of Judah
settings.to: The priests and Levites gathered in the east square
settings.when: The first month of his first year, about 727 or 715 BC, depending on the chronology, after he opened the Temple doors
settings.why: 'Our fathers acted unfaithfully... Now my heart is set on making a covenant.' Hezekiah confesses that the closing of the Temple brought wrath, captivity and loss, and calls the Levites, 'my sons,' to make the house holy. Kings tells his reform in one verse (2 Kings 18:4); Chronicles opens with this speech. For readers whose fathers' sins led to exile, it was a model of confession that leads to new worship.

settings.by: The Levites
settings.to: King Hezekiah
settings.when: On the sixteenth day of the first month
settings.why: The house, the altar, the table and the vessels Ahaz threw out are clean and ready. The report ends sixteen days of work. For readers whose ancestors brought back the Temple vessels from Babylon (Ezra 1:7–11), the restoring of the vessels meant continuity with the first Temple.

settings.what: The praise of David and Asaph and Hezekiah's call
settings.by: The Levites, at the king's order; then Hezekiah
settings.to: The LORD; then the assembly
settings.when: At the rededication
settings.why: The Levites praise 'with the words of David and of Asaph,' that is, with psalms, and Hezekiah calls the people to bring thank offerings. Worship is set in order again 'in a moment.' For readers, the psalms they sang were the same ones sung at Hezekiah's renewal.

title: Return to the LORD
sum: Hezekiah invites all Israel and Judah, from Beersheba to Dan, to keep Passover in Jerusalem. Because the priests and people were not ready, they hold it in the second month. Runners carry his letters through the north: return to the LORD, and he will return to you; he is gracious and compassionate. Many laugh at the messengers, but some from Asher, Manasseh and Zebulun humble themselves and come.

The crowd removes the altars from Jerusalem and keeps the feast. Many from the north eat without being clean, and Hezekiah prays: may the good LORD make atonement for everyone who sets his heart on seeking God. God hears and heals the people. The feast is extended a second week, and there is joy like nothing since Solomon. The priests bless the people, and their prayer reaches heaven.
readings: Read as history

Kings has no Passover under Hezekiah and says Josiah's was the first of its kind since the judges (2 Kings 23:22). Some historians think Hezekiah did invite northern survivors after Samaria's fall; others think Chronicles built the account on Josiah's Passover.
Read as invitation

The chapter is the clearest call to reunion in Chronicles. Its key verb, "return," means both repentance and the return of exiles, and the letter's promise echoes Solomon's prayer. The heart matters more than ritual readiness, and the result is joy.

views.H: Hezekiah reaches out to the remnant of the north, and those who come are received even when they are not ritually clean. The feast shows a united Israel worshiping at one temple.
views.C: Hezekiah's Passover is a Chronicler's creation or expansion, modeled on Solomon's dedication (seven days and seven more) and on Josiah's Passover. It carries a message for the writer's own time: northerners who seek the LORD at Jerusalem are welcome.
views.S: Kings mentions no Passover under Hezekiah. Chronicles' comparison "not since Solomon" (30:26) sits beside Kings' "not since the judges" for Josiah (2 Kings 23:22), which Chronicles keeps in 35:18 as "since Samuel."
views.J: The Mishnah reports that Hezekiah "intercalated Nisan in Nisan" and that the sages did not approve (Mishnah Pesahim 4:9; Bavli Sanhedrin 12a–b). Rabbinic law kept the second Passover of Numbers 9 for individuals, not for the nation.
views.X: Christian readers have heard in Hezekiah's prayer for the unclean (30:18–19) the gospel principle that God looks on the heart. The invitation mocked by many and accepted by few has been compared to Jesus' parable of the banquet (Luke 14:16–24).

deep.b: The Law allowed individuals who were unclean or far away to keep Passover a month late (Numbers 9:9–12). Chronicles gives the same reasons for the nation (30:3). Some scholars suggest another factor: the northern kingdom may have kept its festivals a month later than Judah, as Jeroboam's feast in the eighth month suggests (1 Kings 12:32–33). A second-month Passover would then have suited northern guests. The Mishnah's tradition that Hezekiah added a second Nisan is a different explanation of the same date (Mishnah Pesahim 4:9).

echoes: Numbers 9:9–12; Exodus 34:6; 1 Kings 8:50; 2 Chronicles 7:8–10; 2 Kings 23:21–23; Luke 14:16–24

settings.by: Hezekiah and his officials, carried by runners
settings.to: All Israel and Judah, from Beersheba to Dan, and especially Ephraim and Manasseh
settings.when: In Hezekiah's first year (about 727 or 715 BC, depending on the chronology), for a Passover in the second month
settings.why: 'Israelites, return to the LORD... so that he may come back to those of you who got away.' The letters speak to 'those of you who got away... from the hand of Assyria's kings.' On the later date that means survivors of Samaria's fall; on the earlier date, survivors of the first deportations (2 Kings 15:29). The letters invite northerners to Jerusalem, promise that God is 'gracious and compassionate,' and that captives may return if Israel returns. Many laugh, some come. For the Chronicler's readers this was the book's strongest call to the people of the north in their own day: come to the house in Jerusalem.
views: Some historians think Hezekiah did reach out to northern survivors after 722 BC.
Others think the Chronicler shaped the account from Josiah's Passover (2 Kings 23:21–23), since Kings says nothing like it.

settings.by: Hezekiah
settings.to: The LORD
settings.when: When many northerners ate the Passover without being ritually clean
settings.why: 'May the good LORD make atonement for everyone whose heart is set on seeking God... even without the cleansing.' The king asks God to accept the heart over the rule, and the LORD 'healed the people.' For readers who cared greatly about purity, the prayer said that a seeking heart matters most, and it opened the way for outsiders to join.

settings.by: The Levite priests
settings.to: The people, with their prayer rising to God
settings.when: At the close of the fourteen days of the feast
settings.why: The priests' blessing, probably the one in Numbers 6:24–26, ends the feast, and the text says their prayer reached heaven. It shows readers that the blessing spoken in their Temple was heard.

title: Heaps of Gifts
sum: After the Passover the worshipers go out and smash the shrines throughout Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim and Manasseh. Hezekiah sets the priests and Levites in their divisions and pays for the regular burnt offerings from his own property. He tells the people of Jerusalem to give the priests and Levites their portion, and they bring firstfruits and tithes in heaps, from the third month to the seventh.

The chief priest Azariah tells the king there is enough and to spare. Hezekiah has storerooms prepared, and Levites are appointed to receive and distribute the gifts fairly to priests and Levites in Jerusalem and the towns, including their families. Hezekiah does what is good, right and true, seeking God with all his heart, and he prospers.
readings: Read as history

The chapter reflects the practical side of a temple economy: tithes, storerooms and officials. Some historians think the lists of Levites come from temple records; others see the organization of the writer's own Second Temple day projected back.
Read as model
For post-exilic readers who struggled to support the temple (Nehemiah 13:10–12; Malachi 3:8–10), the chapter shows a generous people, a giving king, and a priesthood that has more than enough.

views.H: Reform includes provision. Hezekiah restores the gifts that sustain worship, and the people's generosity shows their faithfulness.
views.C: The chapter mirrors the concerns of Nehemiah 10 and 13 about tithes and Levite support. Its detailed administration reflects Second Temple structures.
views.S: None of this chapter is in Kings, apart from the destruction of shrines summarized in 2 Kings 18:4.
views.J: The Mishnah tractates Terumot, Maaserot and Bikkurim lay out the laws of gifts and tithes this chapter assumes. Rabbinic tradition held that the tithe was a test in which God invites Israel to try him (Malachi 3:10; Bavli Taanit 9a).
views.X: Christian teaching on giving has used this chapter as a picture of joyful generosity and of a church that provides for its ministers (1 Corinthians 9:13–14; 2 Corinthians 9:6–8).

echoes: Numbers 18:8–32; Deuteronomy 14:22–29; Nehemiah 10:35–39; Nehemiah 13:10–12; Malachi 3:10; 1 Corinthians 9:13–14

settings.what: Hezekiah's order for the priests' and Levites' share
settings.by: Hezekiah
settings.to: The priests and Levites by their divisions; and the people of Jerusalem
settings.when: After the Passover and the removal of the high places
settings.why: The king sets the clergy's divisions and pays for the regular offerings from his own property. He orders the people to give the priests and Levites their share, 'so that they might stay firm in the LORD's law.' The rule answers a practical problem: clergy who are not supported leave their work, as happened in Nehemiah's day (Nehemiah 13:10). For readers it was a call to tithe.

settings.by: Azariah the chief priest, of Zadok's house
settings.to: Hezekiah
settings.when: When the king asked about the heaps of gifts
settings.why: 'We have eaten and been full, and much is left over. The LORD has blessed his people.' The report links generous giving with blessing, an echo of Malachi 3:10. Readers heard that giving to God's house does not leave the giver poor.

traditions.q: Hezekiah's people brought a tenth of everything (2 Chronicles 31:5–6). Must Christians give a tenth?
views: Yes. Seventh-day Adventists teach that the tithe belongs to God and is returned to him to support the gospel ministry, as part of faithful stewardship (Fundamental Beliefs 21).
Yes. A revelation of 1838 made tithing a standing law for church members (Doctrine and Covenants 119), and paying a full tithe is required to enter the temple.
Most Pentecostal churches teach the tithe as the starting point of giving, often citing Malachi 3:10. Some prosperity preachers promise riches in return, a teaching many Pentecostal leaders reject.
The Church asks its members to help provide for its needs, each according to ability (Catechism 2043), but sets no fixed tenth. Some parishes hold up the tithe as a goal.

Many evangelical teachers hold that the tithe belonged to the Law of Moses, which supported the Levites and the temple. They urge giving that is generous, regular and in proportion to income, as Paul does (1 Corinthians 16:2; 2 Corinthians 9:7), with the tenth as a guide, not a rule.

title: An Arm of Flesh
sum: "After these things and this faithfulness," Sennacherib invades Judah. Hezekiah stops up the springs outside Jerusalem, repairs the wall, builds an outer wall, makes weapons, and encourages the people: the one with us is greater; he has an arm of flesh, we have the LORD. Sennacherib's officers mock Hezekiah and his God at the walls, in Judean, and his letters insult the LORD as one of the gods of the nations.

Hezekiah and Isaiah pray, and an angel destroys the Assyrian leaders. Sennacherib goes home in shame and is killed by his sons. Hezekiah falls ill and is given a sign; his heart grows proud, then he humbles himself. He becomes wealthy, channels the Gihon water into the city, and when Babylon's envoys come, God leaves him to test him. He is buried with honor.
readings: Read as history

Sennacherib's campaign of 701 BC is one of the best-documented events in the Bible: Assyrian annals, the Lachish reliefs, Hezekiah's tunnel and the Broad Wall. All agree that Judah was devastated and that Jerusalem was not taken. Chronicles does not mention the tribute both Kings and the annals report.
Read as condensed

Chronicles compresses three chapters of Kings into one, assuming readers know the fuller story. It keeps the threat, the prayer and the deliverance, and turns Hezekiah's illness and the Babylonian envoys into brief notes on pride and testing.

views.H: Faithfulness does not exempt Hezekiah from attack, but it carries him through it. He prepares wisely and trusts God, and God delivers Jerusalem.
views.C: The Chronicler has reshaped Kings to remove any taint from Hezekiah's faithfulness: no tribute, no surrender. The theological framing of 32:1 answers the problem the invasion poses for a theology of reward.
views.S: Kings includes Hezekiah's payment (2 Kings 18:14–16), the Rabshakeh's long speeches, Isaiah's oracles, the 185,000 dead, the healing with the shadow sign and the Babylonian envoys' visit. Chronicles keeps the outline but shortens nearly every scene and adds the water works and wall.
views.J: The Talmud says God wanted to make Hezekiah the messiah and Sennacherib Gog and Magog, but Hezekiah did not sing a song of praise after his rescue (Bavli Sanhedrin 94a). Rabbinic tradition celebrated the night of the deliverance as a Passover night.
views.X: Christian readers have long quoted 32:7–8, "the one with us is greater," alongside 1 John 4:4. The deliverance of Jerusalem is often preached as an example of answered prayer.

deep.b: Three passages describe them: Hezekiah "made the pool and the channel and brought the water into the city" (2 Kings 20:20); he "stopped up the upper outlet of the waters of Gihon and led them straight down, westward" (32:30); and Sirach praises him for digging through rock with iron (Sirach 48:17). The tunnel, 533 meters long and winding, runs from the Gihon spring to the Siloam pool. The inscription found inside in 1880 describes the moment the two teams of diggers heard each other through the rock and broke through. Radiocarbon dates from the plaster fit about 700 BC.

deep.title: Why leave out the tribute?
deep.b: Claude's theory. Chronicles is not hiding the tribute from readers who knew Kings; it assumes they knew it. It may instead be making a point: whatever Hezekiah paid, it was not the payment that saved Jerusalem. The silence turns the story from politics into prayer. Sara Japhet (I and II Chronicles, 1993) and Raymond Dillard (WBC, 1987) already read the omission theologically; what I add is only the stress on readers' knowledge of Kings.

echoes: 2 Kings 18:13–20:21; Isaiah 36:1–39:8; Isaiah 22:9–11; 2 Kings 6:16; Jeremiah 17:5; Deuteronomy 8:2; Sirach 48:17

settings.by: Hezekiah
settings.to: The commanders and people gathered in the square at the city gate
settings.when: As Sennacherib invaded Judah in 701 BC
settings.why: 'He has an arm of flesh. We have the LORD our God.' After stopping the springs and rebuilding the walls, Hezekiah encourages the people with words like those of Moses and David ('Be strong and bold'). Chronicles leaves out Kings' account of Hezekiah's tribute (2 Kings 18:14–16) and gives this speech instead. For readers it put trust at the center of the crisis.

settings.by: Sennacherib king of Assyria, through his servants and in letters
settings.to: Hezekiah and all Judah in Jerusalem; and the people on the wall, in Judean
settings.when: While Sennacherib was at Lachish, 701 BC
settings.why: The same scene as 2 Kings 18:17–19:13, shortened. In Kings the Rabshakeh's long speeches raise the question of trust for exiles who had seen an empire win. Chronicles keeps the core claims: Hezekiah removed the high places, and no god has saved any land. It adds that they spoke of Jerusalem's God 'as they spoke of the gods of the peoples of the earth, things that human hands had made.' For its readers the scene is a contest between the living God and idols, and its answer is already known.

settings.what: The prayer of Hezekiah and Isaiah
settings.by: Hezekiah the king and Isaiah son of Amoz
settings.to: The LORD (the text says they cried out 'to the heavens')
settings.when: After the letters
settings.why: Chronicles sums up in one verse Hezekiah's prayer and Isaiah's oracle (2 Kings 19:14–34), the same scene. Kings gives the full words for exiles who needed them. Chronicles needs only the act: king and prophet pray together, and God answers. For readers it was a picture of leaders turning to prayer first.

settings.what: Hezekiah's prayer in sickness and his repentance
settings.by: Hezekiah
settings.to: The LORD
settings.when: In his illness, and after
settings.why: The same events as 2 Kings 20:1–19, told in three verses. Kings tells of tears, fifteen more years, the shadow on the steps, and Isaiah's oracle of Babylon. Chronicles adds a judgment: his heart 'rose up high,' wrath came, and then he and Jerusalem humbled themselves. The purpose shifts from foreshadowing the exile to showing again the pattern of 7:14.

title: Manasseh in Chains
sum: Manasseh becomes king at twelve and reigns fifty-five years. He rebuilds the high places, sets up altars for Baal and the stars inside the temple courts, burns his sons in the Valley of Ben-hinnom, practices sorcery and places a carved figure in God's house. He leads Judah to do worse than the nations. The LORD speaks, but no one listens.

So Assyria's commanders take Manasseh with hooks to Babylon. In distress he humbles himself and prays, God hears him and brings him back, and he knows that the LORD is God. He builds Jerusalem's outer wall, removes the foreign gods and the figure, restores the LORD's altar and tells Judah to serve the LORD. His son Amon does evil, does not humble himself, and is murdered after two years; the people of the land put Josiah on the throne.
readings: Read as history

Manasseh appears in Assyrian records as a loyal vassal. No source mentions his captivity, but similar treatment of vassals is known, and the Babylonian revolt of 652–648 BC offers a setting. Many historians keep the question open.
Read as theology

Chronicles uses Manasseh as the strongest proof of its message that repentance is possible: if the worst king can humble himself and be restored, so can anyone. The contrast with Kings, which blames him for the exile, is deliberate.

views.H: Manasseh's story is of the worst king's conversion. Captivity brings him to his knees, God answers his prayer, and he spends his last years undoing what he did.
views.C: Most critical scholars think the Chronicler created or expanded the repentance to explain Manasseh's long reign under his theory of retribution, and to offer hope to exiles. Some accept a historical core in an Assyrian summons.
views.S: 2 Kings 21:1–18 has no captivity, prayer or reform; it instead quotes the prophets' doom on Jerusalem because of Manasseh and later says his sins could not be forgiven (2 Kings 24:3–4). Chronicles drops these. Both books share the list of sins almost word for word.
views.J: The Mishnah counts Manasseh among three kings with no share in the world to come; Rabbi Judah disagreed, citing 33:13 (Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:2). The Jerusalem Talmud says God dug a tunnel under his throne to receive Manasseh's prayer when the angels blocked heaven's windows. A tradition held that Manasseh had Isaiah killed.
views.X: The Prayer of Manasseh, in the Orthodox Bible and the Apocrypha, became a classic of Christian penitence and was used in the liturgy. Manasseh appears in Jesus' genealogy (Matthew 1:10), a sign of grace to the undeserving.

deep.b: The prayer Chronicles mentions (33:18–19) is not given. A Greek prayer of fifteen verses in his name appears among the Odes after the Psalms in Codex Alexandrinus and in the Didascalia Apostolorum. It confesses: "I have sinned more than the number of the sand of the sea... and now I bend the knee of my heart." It is part of the Bible of the Eastern Orthodox churches, printed in an appendix to the Latin Vulgate, and placed among the Apocrypha in the KJV and many Protestant editions. A different Hebrew poem headed "Prayer of Manasseh king of Judah" was found at Qumran (4Q381). Neither is likely to be the record Chronicles cites.

echoes: 2 Kings 21:1–26; 2 Kings 23:26; 2 Kings 24:3–4; Deuteronomy 18:10–11; 1 Kings 18:39; Jeremiah 15:4; Ezekiel 18:21–23

settings.what: God's promise for the Temple, quoted
settings.by: God, as quoted by the Chronicler
settings.to: David and Solomon, recalled for the readers
settings.when: Quoted to show what Manasseh's carved image violated
settings.why: The same quotation as 2 Kings 21:7–8. In Kings, read in exile, it shows the condition that Judah broke. In Chronicles, read by those back in the land, the promise 'never again will I remove Israel's feet' has a second life, since they were living on that soil again.

settings.what: The LORD's warning and Manasseh's prayer
settings.by: The LORD; then Manasseh in captivity
settings.to: Manasseh and his people; then the LORD his God
settings.when: During Manasseh's reign, when Assyria's officers took him to Babylon
settings.why: The LORD spoke but they did not listen (Kings gives the words, 2 Kings 21:10–15). Chronicles alone tells that Manasseh, bound in Babylon, humbled himself and prayed, and God brought him back. The prayer's words are not given (the later Prayer of Manasseh fills them in). For readers who had been in Babylon, Manasseh's story was their own: the worst sinner, taken to Babylon, can repent and be brought home. The Talmud debates whether Manasseh has a share in the world to come, and some rabbis cite his prayer as proof that repentance was accepted (Bavli Sanhedrin 101b–103a).
views: Some historians link it to Assyria's crushing of the Babylonian revolt in 652–648 BC, when vassals were summoned.
Many critical scholars: the Chronicler shaped the account to explain Manasseh's long reign and to show that repentance is always possible.

settings.what: Manasseh's order to serve the LORD
settings.by: Manasseh
settings.to: The people of Judah
settings.when: After his return from Babylon
settings.why: He rebuilds the LORD's altar and 'told Judah to serve the LORD.' The command shows a repentant king using his power to undo his own harm, though the people go on using the high places. Readers saw that repentance must be acted out.

traditions.q: Chronicles says Manasseh's prayer was written down but does not give it (2 Chronicles 33:18–19). Is the Prayer of Manasseh Scripture?
views: Greek Orthodox Bibles print it among the Odes after the Psalms, and it is prayed at Great Compline in Lent. The Orthodox churches have never fixed the outer edge of the Old Testament at a council, so its exact rank is not settled.
No. The Council of Trent did not include it in its list (1546). The official Latin Bible of 1592 printed it in an appendix with 1 Esdras and 4 Ezra, so that it would not be lost.
Article 6 lists it among the books the church reads for example of life, but not to establish any doctrine. A canticle drawn from it is sung in Anglican worship.
Luther's Bible of 1534 printed it at the end of the Apocrypha, books not held equal to Holy Scripture but useful and good to read.
No. The Westminster Confession says the books called the Apocrypha are not inspired and have no more authority in the church than other human writings (1.3).

title: The Scroll in the Temple
sum: Josiah becomes king at eight. At sixteen he begins to seek God, and at twenty he purges Judah and Jerusalem, crushing the idols, burning priests' bones on their altars, and carrying the reform to the northern towns. In his eighteenth year, while the temple is being repaired with silver gathered from all Israel, Hilkiah the priest finds the scroll of the LORD's law given through Moses.

When Shaphan reads it, the king tears his clothes and sends to the prophet Huldah. She confirms the curses on Jerusalem but promises Josiah he will be gathered to his grave in peace, because his heart was soft and he humbled himself. Josiah reads the covenant scroll to the people and pledges them all to keep it, and they do not turn away while he lives.
readings: Read as history

The reform is widely dated to the 620s BC, when Assyrian power was fading. The scroll is usually identified with a form of Deuteronomy. Chronicles' order, reform before discovery, may preserve a memory that change began earlier than Kings suggests, or may reflect the writer's theology.
Read as a story of the word

At the center is a scroll found, read and obeyed. The king's response, tearing his clothes and humbling himself, is the model of how to hear God's word, and Huldah's oracle shows that judgment can be delayed for those who listen.

views.H: Josiah is the last good king, who sought God young and responded to the rediscovered law with grief and covenant. His humility earns a reprieve for his lifetime.
views.C: Chronicles has rearranged Kings so that the reform starts before the scroll is found, showing Josiah's piety as his own. Many critical scholars think the scroll, a form of Deuteronomy, was written in Josiah's time to support his program.
views.S: Kings places the whole reform after the scroll's discovery and describes it at length (2 Kings 23:4–20), including Bethel. Chronicles moves the purge before the scroll and summarizes it briefly; the scroll scene and Huldah's oracle are copied closely, with Levites added.
views.J: The Talmud asks why Josiah sent to Huldah rather than Jeremiah, and answers that women are more compassionate (Bavli Megillah 14b). Medieval commentators explained the king's alarm by saying the scroll opened at the curse of exile for king and people (Deuteronomy 28:36).
views.X: Christian reformers often took Josiah as their model: the rediscovery of Scripture leading to the renewal of worship. His tearing of clothes at the hearing of God's word has been used as an image of true conviction.

deep.b: Chronicles has Josiah's reform reach the towns of Manasseh, Ephraim, Simeon and Naphtali (34:6), and silver come from "all the rest of Israel" (34:9). Kings mentions Bethel and "the towns of Samaria" (2 Kings 23:15–20). Archaeologists debate how far Josiah's power reached; some think he took Bethel and the hill country of Benjamin, others that his kingdom grew toward the coast and north as Assyria withdrew. Chronicles treats the reform as a renewal for all Israel.

echoes: 2 Kings 22:1–23:3; 1 Kings 13:2; Deuteronomy 28:15–68; Deuteronomy 31:24–26; Jeremiah 1:2; Zephaniah 1:1

settings.what: Josiah's charge to seek the LORD
settings.by: King Josiah
settings.to: Hilkiah, Ahikam, Abdon, Shaphan and Asaiah
settings.when: After hearing the scroll of the law, his eighteenth year, 622 BC
settings.why: The same scene as 2 Kings 22:12–13, but Josiah asks for 'those left in Israel and in Judah,' and says the LORD's anger 'has poured out on us.' Chronicles thinks of the whole remnant of Israel, north and south. For its readers, the remnant asking God what the law means was a picture of themselves.

settings.by: Huldah the prophet, for the LORD, the God of Israel
settings.to: Josiah's officials, with one word for 'the man who sent you' and another for 'the king of Judah'
settings.when: 622 BC, in Jerusalem's second district
settings.why: The same oracle as 2 Kings 22:15–20, almost word for word, but here 'all the curses written in the scroll.' In Kings it explains to exiles why even Josiah could not stop the end. In Chronicles, where Josiah humbles himself as 7:14 asks, it shows humbling bringing mercy to the one who humbles himself. Both settings face the same problem: Josiah was promised peace and died in battle.
views: Many readers: 'in peace' means before the disaster, which came after Josiah's death.
Some critical scholars: an older oracle kept as it was spoken, even though Josiah later fell at Megiddo.

settings.what: The reading of the covenant scroll and the covenant
settings.by: King Josiah
settings.to: The elders and all the men of Judah and Jerusalem, the priests and the Levites, great and small
settings.when: 622 BC, in the LORD's house
settings.why: The same scene as 2 Kings 23:1–3, except that Chronicles names 'the Levites' where Kings has 'the prophets,' and says Josiah 'made everyone... take their stand.' In Kings the covenant is the high point before the fall. In Chronicles it is a model for the readers' own gatherings to hear the law, led by Levites (Nehemiah 8–10), and it is followed by a lifetime of faithfulness (34:33).

title: No Passover Like It
sum: Josiah keeps the Passover on its proper day. He sets the priests in their posts and tells the Levites to put the ark in Solomon's temple, since they no longer carry it, and to prepare for their brothers. The king gives thirty thousand lambs and kids and three thousand cattle; his officials and the Levite chiefs add more. Levites slaughter and skin, priests splash the blood, the meat is cooked, and singers and gatekeepers keep their places. No Passover like it had been kept since Samuel.

Later Neco of Egypt marches to Carchemish. Josiah goes out to meet him. Neco warns that God has sent him and that Josiah should not oppose God. Josiah disguises himself and fights at Megiddo, is shot by archers, and dies in Jerusalem. Jeremiah laments him, and the laments become a custom in Israel.
readings: Read as history

In 609 BC Neco II marched north to support the last Assyrian king against Babylon. Josiah's attempt to stop him at Megiddo ended in his death. The Babylonian Chronicle confirms the campaign; Kings and Chronicles give different details of his death.
Read as tragedy

The best king of Chronicles dies for not listening. The writer frames his death with phrases from Ahab's (1 Kings 22:30–34), and the man who heard God's word in the scroll misses it in a foreign king's mouth.

views.H: Josiah's reign closes with a Passover of unmatched faithfulness and a death that the narrator explains: even a good king must listen when God speaks.
views.C: Chronicles has expanded Kings' three-verse Passover with the procedures of its own time and explained Josiah's death, which Kings leaves unexplained, as disobedience. The Neco speech is the writer's composition.
views.S: Kings gives the Passover three verses (2 Kings 23:21–23) and the death two (23:29–30), where Neco kills Josiah at Megiddo "when he saw him." Chronicles adds the Levites' roles, Neco's message, the disguise, the wound, the death in Jerusalem and Jeremiah's lament.
views.J: The Talmud says Josiah went out to fight because he trusted Leviticus 26:6, that no sword would pass through a faithful land, not knowing his generation was not faithful (Bavli Taanit 22b). Tradition said he hid the ark before the exile (Bavli Yoma 52b). The Targum to Lamentations reads Lamentations 4:20 of him.
views.X: Christian readers have seen Josiah's death as one of the great tragedies of Scripture. The mourning at Megiddo (Zechariah 12:11) is applied in John 19:37 and Revelation 1:7 to the grief over the pierced one.

deep.b: Exodus requires the Passover lamb to be roasted, never boiled (Exodus 12:9). Deuteronomy says "cook it" with the verb bashal, which elsewhere means boil (Deuteronomy 16:7). Chronicles writes that "they cooked the Passover in the fire, by the rule" (35:13), using Deuteronomy's verb with Exodus' fire, and keeps boiling for the other holy offerings. Scholars see here one of the earliest examples of harmonizing two laws, a method that became central to rabbinic interpretation.

The Greek book called 1 Esdras (Esdras A in the Septuagint; 3 Esdras in the Latin) begins with this Passover and runs through the end of Chronicles, all of Ezra 1–10 and part of Nehemiah 8, with an added story of three young men at the court of Darius. Its text of 2 Chronicles 35–36 (cited here in the numbering of Swete's Greek text; the KJV Apocrypha's numbers run up to three verses higher in chapter 1) often agrees with the Hebrew against the Greek of Chronicles, but has its own readings, such as Josiah ignoring "the words of Jeremiah the prophet from the mouth of the Lord" (1 Esdras 1:26). Josephus used it for his account of the return.

echoes: 2 Kings 23:21–30; Exodus 12:1–11; Deuteronomy 16:1–8; 1 Kings 22:30–34; Zechariah 12:11; Lamentations 4:20; 1 Esdras 1:1–31

settings.what: Josiah's charge to the Levites for Passover
settings.by: King Josiah
settings.to: The Levites 'who taught all Israel and were holy to the LORD'
settings.when: At the Passover of his eighteenth year, 622 BC
settings.why: Kings has one sentence: keep the Passover 'by what is written in this covenant scroll' (2 Kings 23:21), the same occasion. Chronicles gives Josiah a speech to the Levites. Put the ark in the house, since you no longer carry it. Serve by your divisions as David and Solomon wrote. Slaughter the Passover for your brothers. The purpose is to show the Levites' new role in a Temple with no need to carry the ark, a role they held in the readers' Temple.

settings.by: Pharaoh Neco II of Egypt, through messengers
settings.to: Josiah king of Judah
settings.when: 609 BC, as Neco marched north to Carchemish on the Euphrates
settings.why: 'Not against you... God bade me hurry. Leave God alone, who is with me.' The same campaign as 2 Kings 23:29, where Neco says nothing. Chronicles gives him a message and says Josiah 'did not listen to Neco's words from God's mouth.' The best king of the book dies for not listening, and the warning comes from a foreigner. For readers it was a hard lesson: God can speak through a foreign ruler, as he did through Cyrus (36:22–23), and even good leaders must listen.
views: The Chronicler's own view (35:22): the words came 'from God's mouth.'
Some readers, ancient and modern, think Neco only claimed divine backing as kings did, and the Chronicler read it as God's warning after the fact.
Many scholars: the account explains why a righteous king died young, as the book's rule seems to require.

settings.by: Jeremiah, and the singers after him
settings.to: All Judah and Jerusalem, mourning Josiah
settings.when: After Josiah's death at Megiddo, 609 BC
settings.why: The words are not given, but the lament became 'a fixed custom in Israel,' written in 'the Laments.' Readers knew a living practice of mourning Josiah. Josephus says Jeremiah's lament was still known in his day, and Jewish tradition sometimes linked it with the book of Lamentations.

title: Let Him Go Up
sum: Four kings follow in quick succession. Jehoahaz reigns three months before Neco takes him to Egypt and puts his brother Jehoiakim on the throne. Nebuchadnezzar binds Jehoiakim and takes temple articles to Babylon. Jehoiachin reigns three months and is taken to Babylon. Zedekiah reigns eleven years, does not humble himself before Jeremiah, and rebels against Nebuchadnezzar. Priests and people defile the temple and mock the prophets God sent early and often, until there is no cure.

The Chaldean king kills young and old even in the sanctuary, takes everything to Babylon, burns the temple and breaks down the walls. The survivors serve him until Persia rises, and the land rests seventy years, making up for its Sabbaths, as Jeremiah said. Then in Cyrus' first year the LORD stirs his spirit, and he proclaims: the God of the heavens has charged me to build him a house in Jerusalem; whoever is of his people, let him go up.
readings: Read as history

The last kings are known from Kings, Jeremiah and the Babylonian Chronicle, which records the capture of Jerusalem in 597 BC and the appointment of a new king. Cyrus took Babylon in 539 BC. Chronicles compresses fifty years into a few verses and passes over the people left in the land.
Read as ending
Chronicles ends not with exile, as Kings does, but with a summons home. In the Hebrew order it is the last book of the Bible, and its last word, "let him go up," leaves the story open.

views.H: The end comes because people and leaders scorned God's patient warnings. Yet God's word through Jeremiah also set a limit, and at its end God moves a foreign king to send his people home.
views.C: The chapter is a theological summary rather than a history, built on Jeremiah's language and Leviticus 26. The closing verses repeat Ezra 1:1–3 and were probably added to link the books or to give Chronicles a hopeful ending.
views.S: Kings gives the last kings' mothers, the details of the sieges, Zedekiah's blinding, the list of temple bronze, Gedaliah's murder and Jehoiachin's release (2 Kings 23:31–25:30). Chronicles keeps the regnal notices, omits most details, and adds the theology of 36:14–21 and the decree of Cyrus.
views.J: The ninth of Av, the fast for the temple's destruction, remembers these events. The rabbis said the first temple fell for idolatry, immorality and bloodshed (Bavli Yoma 9b). Because Chronicles ends the Hebrew Bible, synagogue readings and modern Zionist writers have heard "let him go up" as a call to aliyah.
views.X: Jesus' lament over Jerusalem (Matthew 23:37) and his parable of the tenants (Mark 12:1–9) echo 36:15–16. Christian Bibles place Chronicles among the histories, so that the Old Testament ends with Malachi; the theme of return from exile has been read as fulfilled in Christ.

deep.b: The Hebrew of Chronicles makes Jehoiachin eight years old; Kings says eighteen (2 Kings 24:8). Kings mentions his wives (2 Kings 24:15), and the Babylonian ration tablets later list rations for "Yaukin, king of Judah" and five of his sons, which suits eighteen. Some manuscripts and versions of Chronicles read eighteen. Most scholars think "ten" fell out of the Hebrew. The site follows the Hebrew of each book and notes the difference.

deep.title: An open ending
deep.b: Claude's theory, largely shared with published work. The Hebrew Bible ends in mid-sentence, as it were: Ezra completes it with "to Jerusalem... and build." Chronicles stops at the invitation. For a book written to people back in the land but still waiting, ending on the call rather than its fulfillment may be deliberate: every generation must decide to go up. Japhet, Williamson and Klein all comment on the open ending and on veya'al; the only thing new here is the claim that the incompleteness was meant.

echoes: 2 Kings 23:31–25:30; Jeremiah 25:11–12; Jeremiah 29:10; Leviticus 26:34–35; Ezra 1:1–4; Isaiah 44:28; Daniel 1:1–2; Daniel 9:2; Matthew 23:37

settings.by: The LORD, through his prophets, sent 'early and often'
settings.to: Zedekiah, the leaders of the priests and the people
settings.when: The last years before 586 BC
settings.why: Not one speech but a summary of all of them. God sent messengers out of pity for his people and his house, and they mocked them 'till there was no cure.' The summary echoes 2 Kings 17:13–14 and Jeremiah 25:4. For readers it gave the reason for the fall in one line: they would not listen.

settings.by: The LORD, through Jeremiah
settings.to: Judah, before and during the exile; recalled for the readers
settings.when: Quoted after the fall of Jerusalem
settings.why: The land rested to make up for its Sabbaths, 'to fill up seventy years.' The Chronicler joins Jeremiah 25:11–12 and 29:10 with the warning of Leviticus 26:34–35. The exile becomes a Sabbath for the land, with a fixed end. For readers it meant that the exile was a pause, not the end.

settings.by: Cyrus king of Persia, roused by the LORD
settings.to: His whole kingdom, by proclamation and in writing; and every one of the LORD's people in it
settings.when: His first year as king of Babylon, 538 BC
settings.why: 'He has appointed me to build him a house in Jerusalem... let him go up.' The same decree as Ezra 1:1–3, where it opens the story of the return. Here it closes the history of the kings, and in the Hebrew order the whole Bible. For the Chronicler's readers, who lived in Jerusalem because of this word, it was both their charter and a standing call to anyone still far off to go up.
views: Bickerman and many historians: a Hebrew form of a real proclamation, framed in the religious terms of the people addressed, as the Cyrus Cylinder does for Babylon.
Some scholars think 36:22–23 was added when the books were arranged, to join Chronicles to Ezra or to end the Bible with hope.
